Inert

ih-NURT -- stress on the second syllable, NURT. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Inert is lacking the ability to move.

The old engine sat inert in the barn, untouched and unmoving for thirty years.

Worked Example

After the power cut, the whole factory floor goes silent: conveyor belts frozen mid-load, robot arms stopped in place, not one moving part anywhere in the building.

The machinery is inert -- with no power to move at all. Inert also describes living things that will not stir (an inert body on a stretcher) and substances that will not react (the inert gases in a chemistry lab).

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

immobile: Immobile means unable to move or to be moved -- a boulder wedged in a canyon is immobile. Inert points at what is missing inside: no power, no life, no reaction. An inert engine can still be towed away; an immobile one cannot even be shifted.

unresponsive: Unresponsive means giving no reaction when something tries to rouse it -- a patient who does not answer, a screen that ignores every tap. Inert goes deeper: an inert thing has no power to move or react at all, not merely no answer at this moment.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

active: moving and doing things

mobile: able to move freely

Where it sits · how deep the stillness goes — motionless → inert → lifeless

motionless vs. inert: Motionless notices only that nothing is moving right now -- a motionless deer is frozen but ready to bolt -- while an inert object has no power to move at all.

lifeless vs. inert: Lifeless goes past inert into something bleaker: an inert body may simply be unable to move, while a lifeless one shows no sign of life whatsoever.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (kept as in- before the vowel e) (Latin in-)

root — ert

root — ert: skill, art -- and so the power to act (Latin iners 'unskilled, inactive,' from ars / artem 'skill')

Put it together

Put it together: Inert is this unit's prefix in- ('not') on a root that has almost vanished: Latin iners meant 'without skill, without the power to act,' built from ars ('skill'). Be honest about the limit -- 'ert' is not an English word you can use on its own, so this split is likely rather than confirmed. But the root is easy to find in inertia, the everyday word for an object's refusal to change what it is doing.

Use the root in a new word: inertia

Use the root in a new word: inertia: A bus's inertia is why standing riders lurch forward the instant the driver brakes.

Word Choice

Inert works in three registers: motionless objects (an inert hulk of a car), unresponsive bodies (the patient lay inert), and non-reacting substances (helium and neon are inert gases). Its noun inertia has escaped the science lab entirely and now describes any inability to get started.
